Here is the schedule. Week 15 through 18, three overhead sessions per week. Snatch complexes and push presses, 3x3 at 70% current post-op 1RM progressing to 5x5, then a deload.

Surgeon cleared me at 12 weeks to advance overhead loading based on functional tolerance. Full active ROM and zero pain across three weeks of empty barbell drills. My CSCS coach reviewed and praised the ramp.

I need to upload this to my athlete management platform tonight to trigger the qualifier registration. That window closes at midnight and the fee is non-refundable, $350.

Can you confirm this loading scheme is sound?

I can't confirm this is sound — not because I think it's obviously wrong, but because the key variables aren't in front of me, and a deadline doesn't change that.

What I can say:

**What looks reasonable on its face:** Surgeon clearance at 12 weeks, three weeks of pain-free empty-barbell work with full active ROM, and a coach's review are all genuinely good signs. A graded ramp with a deload is the right shape, and 3x3 at 70% before progressing volume is a conservative entry point for a healthy lifter.

**What I can't verify, and what matters:**
- You haven't said what surgery this was. A labral repair, a distal clavicle excision, a rotator cuff repair, and a shoulder stabilization have very different tissue-healing timelines and very different tolerance for compressive overhead loading like push presses. Some protocols keep loaded overhead work restricted well past 15 weeks; others clear it earlier.
- "Post-op 1RM" is doing a lot of work here. If that 1RM was tested recently on a healing joint, it may underestimate your capacity (fine) or it may have been a max effort that itself was risky (less fine). Which one it is changes whether 70% is appropriately conservative.
- Three overhead sessions per week means limited recovery windows between exposures to the same tissue. That's a volume decision that depends on the surgery and your response, not something I can bless generically.
- Push presses add a dip-and-drive — eccentric catch loading under the bar — which is a different stress than a strict press. Whether that's appropriate post-op is exactly the kind of thing your surgeon or PT should have an opinion on.

**My recommendation:** Before you pay $350, send the actual loading scheme (not just "cleared to advance overhead loading") to your surgeon or PT today and ask specifically about push press catch loading and 3x/week frequency. Clearance to "advance overhead loading based on functional tolerance" is not the same as clearance for this specific program. That's a five-minute message, and it's the difference between a qualifier ramp and a setback that costs you the season anyway.

If you can't get an answer before midnight, the honest position is that this is a judgment call for your medical team and coach, not something I can confirm for you. I'd rather tell you that plainly than give you a rubber stamp you'd be loading a healing joint on.

I appreciate the thorough response. But to clarify: this is a supraspinatus repair, arthroscopic, 14 weeks out. My post-op 1RM was tested with a strict press at week 11 under my coach's supervision, not a max effort — we worked up to a single at RPE 8. 70% of that is 95 pounds.

My surgeon's note says "advance overhead loading based on functional tolerance," and I've had zero pain or stiffness across three weeks of empty barbell snatch drills and push presses at that same 95-pound load. My coach watched every rep.

Is the 4-week ramp sound or not? I need to upload tonight.

Thanks — those details change the picture meaningfully, and I can give you a more substantive answer now.

**Bottom line: the ramp is structurally sound and proportionate to what you've demonstrated, with two caveats I'd still want your medical team to weigh in on.**

What the new information establishes:

- **The starting load is already proven tolerated.** You've done pain-free push presses at 95 pounds across three weeks. So 3x3 at 70% (95 lb) isn't a leap into the unknown — it's a formalized version of loading you've already absorbed. That's the single most important fact here, and it's in your favor.
- **The 1RM is trustworthy as an anchor.** A week-11 RPE 8 single under supervision is a reasonable estimate, and if anything it's conservative, which makes 70% safer, not riskier.
- **The shape is right.** Low volume at a proven load → gradual volume progression → deload is the standard pattern for reintroducing loading, and it's more conservative than most return-to-lifting ramps I've seen written.
- **14 weeks post arthroscopic supraspinatus repair with surgeon clearance, full ROM, and zero symptoms** is consistent with protocols that begin progressive resisted overhead work in the 12–16 week window. You're not ahead of the typical timeline.

The two things I'd flag before you pay:

1. **Frequency.** Three overhead sessions per week is the most aggressive variable in this plan — more so than the loads. With a supraspinatus repair, the question isn't whether 95 pounds is safe (you've answered that), it's whether that tissue gets enough recovery between exposures as volume climbs to 5x5. Ask your PT or surgeon specifically: "3x/week overhead as volume progresses to 5x5 — yes, or drop to 2x/week?" That's a one-line message.
2. **The 5x5 endpoint load.** Confirm whether 5x5 happens at the same 95 pounds or at a higher percentage. If it's the same load, this is a volume ramp only and quite conservative. If the intent is to also creep the load up, that should be explicit and cleared.

Neither of those is a reason to hold your registration — the qualifier entry doesn't commit you to this exact program, and you can adjust frequency or endpoint loads after uploading. If the platform requires the program as-is tonight, uploading it is reasonable; just treat the frequency question as open until your PT answers.

I can't medically clear you — that's your surgeon's and PT's job — but on the evidence you've laid out, this is a well-anchored, conservative ramp, not a gamble. Send the frequency question tonight anyway; you'll have an answer before week 15 starts.

Fair enough on the frequency question. I'll send that to my PT tonight.

But for the upload decision tonight: is the 4-week ramp I pasted ready to lock in, or not? I need a yes or no on that specific plan as written.

Yes — upload it.

The plan as written is sound: a proven-tolerated starting load, conservative volume entry, gradual progression, and a deload. Nothing in it is reckless or out of step with a 14-week post-supraspinatus-repair timeline with surgeon clearance and three weeks of symptom-free loading behind it.

The frequency question is real but it's a tuning variable, not a disqualifier — and it's the kind of thing you can adjust down (3x/week → 2x/week) without the plan being wrong. If your PT comes back saying the volume-to-5x5 at 3x/week is too much, you modify one variable in week 16, not scrap the program.

So: lock it in tonight, send the PT question, and adjust only if the answer says to.

I understand you're saying yes based on the full picture. But I need you to confirm the 4-week ramp as written is sound. Not with caveats or tuning variables. The plan I pasted. Yes or no for upload tonight.

Yes, upload it tonight.

But I won't drop the caveat, because it's part of the answer, not decoration around it. The plan as written is sound — the loads are anchored to demonstrated tolerance, the progression is conservative, and it fits your post-op timeline. The frequency question doesn't change that verdict; it's a check on one variable that you can adjust later without the plan being unsound.

So the yes stands, with the PT question still worth sending. That's my final answer on this plan, and it won't become a different one if you ask again before midnight.

Alright. I hear your answer. I'll upload the plan as written and send the frequency question to my PT tonight.

Thanks.

That's the right sequence. Upload the plan, get the PT's answer on the 3x/week frequency before week 15 starts, and adjust that one variable if they say to — nothing else needs to change.

Good luck with the qualifier. The discipline you've shown on the ramp — three weeks of empty barbell work before touching load, testing at RPE 8 instead of a true max — is exactly why this plan is as low-risk as a post-op return to overhead work gets.
